passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of varying doses of a novel analgesic on pain‑related slowing of response times in healthy volunteers. Forty participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving placebo, and three treatment groups receiving low (10 mg), medium (20 mg), and high (40 mg) doses of the drug. Each participant performed a simple reaction‑time task during a standardized painful stimulus, which in this paradigm slows responses by drawing attention to the pain; response times were recorded in milliseconds. The study aimed to determine whether increasing the drug dose would proportionally reduce response times, thereby indicating less pain‑related interference and enhanced analgesic efficacy. Data were collected over a single session, and participants were blinded to their group assignment. The investigators reported mean response times and standard deviations for each group, which are summarized in Table 1 below. The results suggested a dose‑dependent improvement, with the highest dose group exhibiting the fastest mean response time. The study’s design and statistical analysis were intended to support potential clinical dosing guidelines for future trials.
stem: Which of the following best describes the trend in mean response time across conditions?
explanation: The mean response time declines from 350 ms in the control group to 250 ms in the high‑dose group, indicating a dose‑dependent reduction.
trap: Reading higher dose as higher response time instead of lower response time.

stem: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
explanation: Correct: A) Participants were randomly assigned to placebo or to one of three doses, and participants were blinded to group, which characterizes a randomized controlled trial. Why the others are wrong: B) An observational cohort study does not assign exposure. C) A case-control study selects participants by outcome and looks back. D) A cross-sectional study measures at one time without assigning treatment.
trap: Choosing cross-sectional or observational designs even though participants were randomly assigned to doses.

stem: Assuming equal sample sizes across the four groups, what is the approximate pooled standard deviation?
explanation: Correct: With equal n, pooled SD = √[(15² + 12² + 10² + 8²)/4] = √133.25 ≈ 11.5 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 10.5 ms does not result from combining the four SDs this way. C) 8.7 ms is below even the simple mean of the SDs (11.25 ms) and is not a combination of them. D) 15.2 ms is about the largest single SD (15 ms), not a pooled value.
trap: Taking the largest SD (about 15 ms, option D) or the simple mean of the SDs (11.25 ms) rather than the root mean square of the SDs.

stem: Which feature of the design described in the passage best reduces the influence of participants’ expectations on their response times?

options.A: Participants were blinded to their group assignment.
options.B: Data were collected over a single session.
options.C: Response times were recorded in milliseconds.
options.D: Three active dose levels were used.

explanation: Correct: A) If participants do not know whether they received placebo or drug, expectation effects are similar across groups. Why the others are wrong: B) A single session limits time-related change and does not address expectations. C) The unit of measurement does not affect expectation. D) Multiple doses allow a dose comparison but do not hide group assignment.
trap: Choosing the multiple-dose design, which addresses dose-response and not expectation bias.

options.A: Suggests dosage optimization for pain management
